conceptTag: A team with too much work in progress
readerTitle: Thirty-one projects started, almost none finished
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사내 마케팅·디자인팀, 리모델링 시공업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 일이 늦어지는 이유는 사람이 부족해서가 아니라 동시에 시작한 일이 너무 많아서일 수 있다. 시작을 줄이면 끝나는 속도가 빨라진다.
misconception: 모두가 바쁘게 여러 일을 동시에 진행하면 전체 일이 더 빨리 끝난다. 일이 밀리면 사람을 더 뽑는 것이 첫 번째 해법이다.

sources.text: 린(Lean) 운영의 표준 개념 (흐름, 진행 중 작업 제한, 가동률과 대기의 관계)

factChecks.note: 카드 3 계산: 1인당 프로젝트 5개, 각 3일 작업. 번갈아 진행하면 총 15일 후 거의 동시에 끝남(전환 비용 제외). 하나씩 끝내면 3, 6, 9, 12, 15일에 완료, 평균 (3+6+9+12+15) ÷ 5 = 9일. 첫 완료는 15일이 아니라 3일.
팀 수치: 6명, 진행 중 31건(1인당 약 5건). 31 ÷ 6 = 5.2이므로 '약 5개'로 표기했습니다.
시공업체 수치: 4개 팀, 진행 중 14건, 팀당 최대 2건이면 동시 진행 8건. 모두 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Thirty-one projects started, almost none finished
body: An in-house marketing team of six people has 31 projects marked *in progress*. Brochures, a product video, three landing pages, a trade-show booth.
Everyone is busy from nine to six. Nobody is slacking. Yet in the last month, the team shipped two things, and the sales team is losing patience.

image.label: A task board overflowing with cards in the 'In progress' column
image.brief: 사무실 벽의 작업 보드. 'To do'와 'Done' 칸은 거의 비어 있고 'In progress' 칸에만 포스트잇이 넘쳐 바닥까지 떨어짐. 그 앞에 바쁘게 움직이는 6명의 팀원. 실제 회사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run this team. What do you change first?
body: Your boss offers budget for one fix. Requests keep arriving at about the same pace as before.
Which move gets finished work out the door fastest?

options.text: Hire a freelancer to add capacity
options.feedback: More hands help a little, but the freelancer joins the same pile of 31 half-done projects. The work still doesn't flow; it just spreads across seven people.

options.text: Stop starting new projects until the open ones drop to about two per person
options.feedback: This is **flow** at work: value reaches the business only when something is finished. Fewer open projects means each one moves through faster.

options.text: Work on whichever request is most urgent that day
options.feedback: It feels responsive, but it adds more switching and leaves even more projects half done. Yesterday's urgent request becomes today's stalled one.

cards.title: One person, five projects, two ways to work.
body: Each project needs about 3 days of real work. Same person, same 15 days of effort. Finishing one at a time cuts the average wait from **15 days to 9**, before even counting the time lost to switching.

breakdown.label: Juggle all five
breakdown.detail: A bit of each every day. All five finish around day 15.

breakdown.label: Finish one first
breakdown.detail: The first project is done on day 3, not day 15

breakdown.label: Average wait, one at a time

cards.title: Started work is not progress.
body: **Flow** means work moves steadily from start to finish without piling up in the middle. A half-made brochure helps no one. It only counts once it's printed.
With 31 projects open, the team's effort is spread so thin that very little crosses the finish line. The fix is simple to say and hard to do: *stop starting, start finishing.*
cards.softwareNote: In software teams, the same pile shows up as dozens of half-built features and open code changes. A feature earns nothing until it's released, so limiting work in progress often speeds up releases more than adding engineers.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · The utilization trap
cards.title: Everyone busy is the warning sign.
body: The team looks efficient because no one has a free minute. That's **the utilization trap**: when people are booked near 100%, every new request waits in line, and waits grow fast.
A team running at about 80% can absorb a surprise rush order. A team at 100% pushes it to the back of 31 other things. Some slack isn't laziness. It's what keeps work moving.

image.label: Two lanes: a jammed full lane and a flowing lane with gaps
image.brief: 두 개의 도로 비교 일러스트. 왼쪽 'Booked 100%' 차선은 차가 빽빽해 멈춰 있음. 오른쪽 'Booked ~80%' 차선은 차 사이에 간격이 있고 화살표처럼 매끄럽게 흐름. 단순한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Now it's a renovation contractor.
body: You run four crews that remodel kitchens and bathrooms. You have 14 jobs open at once. Customers complain their homes have sat half-finished for weeks.
Three new customers want to start next month. What do you do?

options.text: Accept all three so every crew stays fully booked
options.feedback: This is the utilization trap. Full schedules feel safe, but every job waits longer, and one delayed delivery stalls everything behind it.

options.text: Cap each crew at two open jobs and start a new one only when one finishes
options.feedback: That's flow. Kitchens finish sooner, crews travel less, and new customers get an honest start date instead of a half-done room.

options.text: Accept all three and rotate crews so every home sees some progress each week
options.feedback: Customers see activity, which calms them for a while. But every job takes longer, and the time lost driving between homes grows.

cards.title: A limit only works if someone holds it.
body: Limiting open work doesn't make requests disappear. They wait in a visible queue instead of a hidden pile. That's better, because you can now choose what goes next. But someone must say *not yet* to colleagues or customers.
Set the limit too low and people sit idle when a job is blocked by a missing part or a late approval. Start with a limit a little below today's level, then adjust.

cards.title: Finish more by starting less.
body: **Concepts used:** *Flow* showed why finished work matters more than started work. *The utilization trap* showed why a team booked at 100% makes everything wait.
**Try it today:** count the projects your team has open right now. Pick a limit below that number and start nothing new until you're under it.
